claim: The metazoan endoplasmic reticulum (ER) serves as a hub for maturation of secreted proteins.
source: The metazoan endoplasmic reticulum (ER) serves both as a hub for maturation of secreted proteins and as an intracellular calcium storage compartment, facilitating calcium-release-dependent cellular processes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ER function in metazoan cells.

claim: The metazoan endoplasmic reticulum (ER) serves as an intracellular calcium storage compartment.
source: The metazoan endoplasmic reticulum (ER) serves both as a hub for maturation of secreted proteins and as an intracellular calcium storage compartment, facilitating calcium-release-dependent cellular processes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ER function in metazoan cells.

claim: ER calcium depletion robustly activates the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: ER calcium depletion robustly activates the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Calcium selectively affects the dynamics of the abundant metazoan ER Hsp70 chaperone BiP by enhancing its affinity for ADP.
source: Here, we report that calcium selectively affects the dynamics of the abundant metazoan ER Hsp70 chaperone BiP, by enhancing its affinity for ADP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: In the calcium-replete ER, ADP rebinding to post-ATP hydrolysis BiP-substrate complexes competes with ATP binding during both spontaneous and co-chaperone-assisted nucleotide exchange, favouring substrate retention.
source: In the calcium-replete ER, ADP rebinding to post-ATP hydrolysis BiP-substrate complexes competes with ATP binding during both spontaneous and co-chaperone-assisted nucleotide exchange, favouring substrate retention.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In the calcium-depleted ER, relative acceleration of ADP-to-ATP exchange favours substrate release.
source: Conversely, in the calcium-depleted ER, relative acceleration of ADP-to-ATP exchange favours substrate release.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of animal cells maintains a high concentration of calcium (Ca2+) compared to the surrounding cytoplasm.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of animal cells is distinct in maintaining a high concentration of calcium (Ca2+) compared to the surrounding cytoplasm (Alvarez and Montero, 2002; Bygrave and Benedetti, 1996; Meldolesi and Pozzan, 1998; Solovyova and Verkhratsky, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Transient Ca2+ release from the ER during signalling events controls numerous processes including gene expression and exocytosis.
source: Transient Ca2+ release from the ER during signalling events controls numerous processes including gene expression and exocytosis (Carreras-Sureda et al., 2018; Raffaello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations that deplete ER Ca2+ activate transducers of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: It has long been known that pharmacological manipulations (Macer and Koch, 1988; Welch et al., 1983; Wong et al., 1993; Wu et al., 1981) and even physiological cues that deplete ER Ca2+ (Sans et al., 2002) activate transducers of the unfolded protein response (UPR), but the role of proteostatic challenge in UPR activation under these conditions remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Physiological cues that deplete ER Ca2+ activate transducers of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: It has long been known that pharmacological manipulations (Macer and Koch, 1988; Welch et al., 1983; Wong et al., 1993; Wu et al., 1981) and even physiological cues that deplete ER Ca2+ (Sans et al., 2002) activate transducers of the unfolded protein response (UPR), but the role of proteostatic challenge in UPR activation under these conditions remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The folded state of the low-density lipoprotein receptor is stabilised by binding Ca2+ as a ligand.
source: The folded state of some ER clients, like the low-density lipoprotein receptor (Fass et al., 1997), is stabilised by binding Ca2+ as a ligand.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Components of the ER protein folding machinery have low-affinity Ca2+-binding sites, whose occupancy is likely to decrease upon ER Ca2+ depletion within the physiological range.
source: Components of the ER protein folding machinery have low-affinity Ca2+-binding sites, whose occupancy is likely to decrease upon ER Ca2+ depletion within the physiological range.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and inference about the properties of ER protein folding machinery components.

claim: The lectin-like chaperones calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) have low-affinity Ca2+-binding sites.
source: Examples are the lectin-like chaperones calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) (Baksh and Michalak, 1991; Wada et al., 1991), Grp94 (Macer and Koch, 1988; Van et al., 1989), and protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) (Lebeche et al., 1994; Lucero et al., 1994; Macer and Koch, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Grp94 has low-affinity Ca2+-binding sites.
source: Examples are the lectin-like chaperones calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) (Baksh and Michalak, 1991; Wada et al., 1991), Grp94 (Macer and Koch, 1988; Van et al., 1989), and protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) (Lebeche et al., 1994; Lucero et al., 1994; Macer and Koch, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) has low-affinity Ca2+-binding sites.
source: Examples are the lectin-like chaperones calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) (Baksh and Michalak, 1991; Wada et al., 1991), Grp94 (Macer and Koch, 1988; Van et al., 1989), and protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) (Lebeche et al., 1994; Lucero et al., 1994; Macer and Koch, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The core functions of CNX, CRT, Grp94, and PDI as chaperones or oxidoreductases are not known to be measurably affected at Ca2+ levels expected in the depleted ER.
source: These low-affinity binding sites are often found on N- or C-terminal extensions of the aforementioned proteins, a feature consistent with the observation that their core functions as chaperones or oxidoreductases are not known to be measurably affected at Ca2+ levels expected in the depleted ER.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and inference about the properties of these proteins.

claim: Release of ER Ca2+ has long been known to correlate with disruption of certain BiP-substrate complexes.
source: Release of ER Ca2+ has long been known to correlate with disruption of certain BiP-substrate complexes (Suzuki et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dissociation of BiP from substrates upon ER Ca2+ depletion occurs very rapidly, on the time-scale of minutes.
source: Such dissociation occurs very rapidly, on the time-scale of minutes (Preissler et al., 2015), which is inconsistent with a process driven by the slow build-up of competing unfolded newly synthesised proteins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ER Ca2+ depletion is associated with the appearance of more BiP oligomers.
source: ER Ca2+ depletion is also associated with the appearance of more BiP oligomers (Preissler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Treatment of a CHO-K1 cell line stably expressing the TCRα reporter with thapsigargin led to a conspicuous increase of the FLAG-M1 signal, consistent with retention of the reporter in the ER under normal conditions and its Ca2+ depletion-induced migration to the cell surface.
source: Treatment of a CHO-K1 cell line stably expressing the TCRα reporter with thapsigargin (Tg; an agent that causes selective loss of ER Ca2+ by inhibiting the ER Ca2+ pump SERCA; Sagara and Inesi, 1991; Thastrup et al., 1990) led to a conspicuous increase of the FLAG-M1 signal, consistent with retention of the reporter in the ER under normal conditions and its Ca2+ depletion-induced migration to the cell surface (Figure 1B), as previously noted (Suzuki et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Both wild-type TCRα and TCRα-N/Q co-immunoprecipitated with BiP and the interaction was slightly but consistently diminished in Tg-treated cells.
source: Importantly, both wild-type TCRα and TCRα-N/Q co-immunoprecipitated with BiP and the interaction was slightly but consistently diminished in Tg-treated cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Addition of ATP to the cell lysates strongly decreased co-precipitation of both TCRα reporters with BiP, consistent with their binding to BiP as typical substrates.
source: Addition of ATP to the cell lysates strongly decreased co-precipitation of both reporters with BiP, consistent with their binding to BiP as typical substrates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and inference based on known properties of BiP.

claim: More BiP was bound to TCRα-N/Q compared to the wild-type version, suggesting that the fate of the mutant reporter more strongly depends on its association with BiP.
source: Although expressed at lower levels, more BiP was bound to TCRα-N/Q compared to the wild-type version, suggesting that the fate of the mutant reporter more strongly depends on its association with BiP (Figure 1C, compare lanes 2 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and inference about the reporter's dependence on BiP.

claim: Tg-induced progression of the reporters to the plasma membrane was blocked by brefeldin A.
source: This interpretation was further corroborated by the observation that Tg-induced progression of the reporters to the plasma membrane was blocked by brefeldin A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which disrupts vesicular transport between ER and the Golgi apparatus (Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Reporter exposure on the cell surface accrued gradually over several hours.
source: Moreover, reporter exposure on the cell surface accrued gradually over several hours (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with the kinetics of vesicular transport between ER and the cell surface (Chen et al., 2013; Hirschberg et al., 1998; Suzuki et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of ER Ca2+ with the ionophore A23187 led to accumulation of the TCRα-N/Q reporter on the cell surface.
source: Depletion of ER Ca2+ with the ionophore A23187 also led to accumulation of the reporter on the cell surface (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The TCRα-N/Q reporter remained intracellular upon treatment with tunicamycin (Tm) or 2-deoxyglucose (2DG).
source: In contrast, the reporter remained intracellular upon treatment with tunicamycin (Tm) or 2-deoxyglucose (2DG) — compounds that cause protein misfolding in the ER by interfering with N-glycosylation (Kozutsumi et al., 1988; Kurtoglu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to prior literature.

claim: Treatment of cells with Tm before addition of Tg diminished ER Ca2+ depletion-induced reporter exposure on the cell surface.
source: Treatment of cells with Tm before addition of Tg diminished ER Ca2+ depletion-induced reporter exposure on the cell surface (Figure 1E, compare bars 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of basal PERK activity diminished ER Ca2+ depletion-induced reporter exposure on the cell surface.
source: Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of basal PERK activity, which increases substrate protein load in the ER by dysregulating the influx of newly synthesised proteins (Harding et al., 2012), had a similar effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The combined application of Tm and PERK inhibitor almost fully blocked subsequent Tg-induced reporter trafficking.
source: The combined application of Tm and PERK inhibitor almost fully blocked subsequent Tg-induced reporter trafficking (Figure 1E, bar 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both Ca2+-depleting agents and glycosylation inhibitors robustly activated the UPR.
source: However, despite their divergent effects on reporter redistribution, both Ca2+-depleting agents and glycosylation inhibitors robustly activated the UPR (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplemnet 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: BiP consists of an N-terminal nucleotide binding domain (NBD) and C-terminal substrate binding domain (SBD) connected by a hydrophobic linker peptide.
source: Like typical Hsp70s, BiP consists of an N-terminal nucleotide binding domain (NBD) and C-terminal substrate binding domain (SBD) connected by a hydrophobic linker peptide (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BiP structure, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In the ATP-bound state, the NBD and SBD of BiP are docked against each other and the SBD adopts an open conformation, allowing fast exchange of substrates.
source: In the ATP-bound state, the NBD and SBD are docked against each other and the SBD adopts an open conformation, allowing fast exchange of substrates.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BiP's chaperone cycle.

claim: ATP hydrolysis to ADP causes domain undocking and closure of the SBD, leading to tight substrate binding.
source: ATP hydrolysis to ADP causes domain undocking and closure of the SBD, leading to tight substrate binding.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BiP's chaperone cycle.

claim: Addition of CaCl2 (to reactions containing magnesium; Mg2+) did not significantly alter BiP's basal ATPase rate but inhibited its JDP-stimulated activity by ∼30%.
source: Addition of CaCl2 (to reactions containing magnesium; Mg2+) did not significantly alter BiP's basal ATPase rate but inhibited its JDP-stimulated activity by ∼30% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of 0.5 mM ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=4) titration of CaCl2 showed a clear inhibitory effect on BiP's ATPase activity, lowering the average ATPase rate of BiP by ∼44% at the highest [CaCl2].
source: However, in the presence of 0.5 mM ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=4) titration of CaCl2 showed a clear inhibitory effect, lowering the average ATPase rate of BiP by ∼44% at the highest [CaCl2].
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ca2+-dependent inhibition of BiP's ATPase activity was slightly enhanced at 1 mM ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), with a reduction by ∼51%.
source: Ca2+-dependent inhibition was slightly enhanced at 1 mM ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), with a reduction by ∼51%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of 3 mM MgCl2, the basal rate of MABA-ADP release from BiP (koff 0.0865 ± 0.0045 s−1) was similar to values reported earlier.
source: In the presence of 3 mM MgCl2, the basal rate of MABA-ADP release from BiP (koff 0.0865 ± 0.0045 s−1) was similar to values reported earlier (Figure 3A; Mayer et al., 2003; Preissler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior literature.

claim: When CaCl2 was added during the dissociation phase, it had little effect on MABA-ADP release from BiP.
source: When added during the dissociation phase, CaCl2 (up to 1 mM) had little effect on MABA-ADP release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When CaCl2 was included alongside the MABA-ADP (and 3 mM MgCl2) during the loading phase, Ca2+ strongly inhibited release in the subsequent dissociation step (decreasing the koff to 0.0171 ± 0.0004 s−1).
source: However, when included alongside the MABA-ADP (and 3 mM MgCl2) during the loading phase, Ca2+ strongly inhibited release in the subsequent dissociation step (decreasing the koff to 0.0171 ± 0.0004 s−1) (Figure 3A, compare traces 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Titrating CaCl2 during MABA-ADP binding to BiP (in the presence of 3 mM MgCl2) yielded a half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 82.3 ± 16.4 µM.
source: Importantly, titrating CaCl2 during MABA-ADP binding to BiP (in the presence of 3 mM MgCl2) yielded a half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 82.3 ± 16.4 µM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The IC50 of 82.3 ± 16.4 µM for Ca2+ inhibition of MABA-ADP release from BiP fits well into the estimated range of physiological free Ca2+ fluctuations in the ER (from >100 µM to low micromolar concentrations).
source: This value fits well into the estimated range of physiological free Ca2+ fluctuations in the ER (from >100 µM to low micromolar concentrations) and suggests that this effect could indeed be relevant to BiP function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental IC50 value and established knowledge about ER Ca2+ concentrations.

claim: Grp170 enhanced nucleotide release from BiP and its net stimulatory effect was considerably greater when BiP•MABA-ADP complexes were formed in the presence of CaCl2 (∼3.1-fold [Mg2+ alone] vs. ∼11.1-fold [Ca2+ and Mg2+]).
source: The NEF, Grp170, enhanced nucleotide release and its net stimulatory effect was considerably greater when BiP•MABA-ADP complexes were formed in the presence of CaCl2 (∼3.1-fold [Mg2+ alone] vs. ∼11.1-fold [Ca2+ and Mg2+]; Figure 3A, compare traces 1 and 4 as well as 3 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Ca2+-containing samples, the dissociation of MABA-ADP from wild-type BiP was slower, while the association rate was slightly enhanced, resulting in a ∼86% lower dissociation constant (KD) for ADP binding to BiP in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Mg2+.
source: In Ca2+-containing samples, the dissociation of MABA-ADP from wild-type BiP was again slower, while the association rate was slightly enhanced, resulting in a ∼86% lower dissociation constant (KD) for ADP binding to BiP in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Mg2+ (Figure 3C, grey bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MABA-ATP dissociation from BiPT229A was unaffected by Ca2+, but its association was conspicuously slower, leading to a ∼3.2-fold higher KD for MABA-ATP binding to BiP in the presence of Ca2+.
source: MABA-ATP dissociation from BiPT229A was unaffected by Ca2+, but its association was conspicuously slower, leading to a ∼3.2-fold higher KD for MABA-ATP binding to BiP in the presence of Ca2+ (Figure 3C, blue bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ca2+ has opposite effects on the binding of ADP and ATP to BiP: it enhances BiP's affinity for ADP while decreasing the affinity for ATP.
source: Thus, Ca2+ has opposite effects on the binding of ADP and ATP to BiP: it enhances BiP's affinity for ADP while decreasing the affinity for ATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ca2+ and Mg2+ bind cooperatively with ADP or ATP to BiP (each in a 1:1 stoichiometry) and both cations occupy the same or overlapping sites in the NBD.
source: It has been proposed, based on differential scanning and isothermal titration calorimetry data, that Ca2+ and Mg2+ bind cooperatively with ADP or ATP to BiP (each in a 1:1 stoichiometry) and that both cations occupy the same or overlapping sites in the NBD (Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ca2+'s effect on BiP is played out during BiP•nucleotide complex formation rather than by cation swap on existing BiP•nucleotide complexes.
source: Moreover, the nucleotide release experiments presented here indicate that Ca2+'s effect is played out during BiP•nucleotide complex formation rather than by cation swap on existing BiP•nucleotide complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Fast recruitment of BiP was observed in the presence of ATP and Mg2+ in the BLI assay.
source: Fast recruitment of BiP was observed in the presence of ATP and Mg2+ (Figure 4A, traces 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BiP recruitment in the BLI assay was dependent on J-domain-stimulated ATP hydrolysis, as the BiP binding signal was weak in the presence of a non-functional J-domain (JQPD).
source: This interaction was dependent on J-domain-stimulated ATP hydrolysis, as the BiP binding signal was weak in the presence of a non-functional J-domain (JQPD) (Figure 4A, trace six and Preissler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and a citation to prior literature.

claim: BiP recruitment in the BLI assay was also efficient in the presence of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3), suggesting that Ca2+ competes only weakly with Mg2+ under these conditions.
source: Although slightly slower, BiP recruitment was also efficient in the presence of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3), suggesting that Ca2+ competes only weakly with Mg2+ under these conditions (Figure 4A, trace 2); consistent with slower cooperative binding of CaATP to BiP, compared to MgATP, and the absence of an allosteric effect of Ca2+ on ATP binding- and hydrolysis-dependent substrate interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and inference about the mechanism.

claim: In Mg2+-containing solutions, BiP dissociation from BLI sensors was slow in the presence of ADP and fast in the presence of ATP.
source: Accordingly, in Mg2+-containing solutions, BiP dissociation was slow in the presence of ADP and fast in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When present in the dissociation phase, the combination of Mg2+ and Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) did not affect the rate of ATP-induced BiP dissociation from sensors.
source: When present in the dissociation phase, the combination of Mg2+ and Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) did not affect the rate of ATP-induced BiP dissociation from sensors (Figure 4A, trace 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dissociation of BiP from BLI sensors was fast in a solution containing ATP and Ca2+ as the only divalent cation, indicating that CaATP is able to allosterically trigger BiP dissociation from its substrates.
source: Dissociation of BiP was also fast in a solution containing ATP and Ca2+ as the only divalent cation, indicating that CaATP is able to allosterically trigger BiP dissociation from its substrates (Figure 4A, trace 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and inference about the mechanism.

claim: In the presence of Mg2+ and both ATP and ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), the dissociation of BiP from J-domain- and P15-coated BLI sensors was slower compared to a solution containing only Mg2+ and ATP, consistent with direct competition of ADP with ATP for binding to BiP.
source: In the presence of Mg2+ and both ATP and ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), the dissociation of BiP from J-domain- and P15-coated BLI sensors was slower compared to a solution containing only Mg2+ and ATP, consistent with direct competition of ADP with ATP for binding to BiP (Figure 4B, trace 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) to a solution containing both nucleotides further inhibited dissociation of BiP from BLI sensors.
source: Addition of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) to a solution containing both nucleotides further inhibited dissociation of BiP (Figure 4B, trace 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BiP bound to a sensor that had been exposed to Mg2+ and ADP dissociated twice as fast in the second step than BiP on a sensor that had been exposed to Ca2+ and ADP.
source: BiP bound to a sensor that had been exposed to Mg2+ and ADP dissociated twice as fast in the second step than BiP on a sensor that had been exposed to Ca2+ and ADP (Figure 4B, compare traces 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The slow release of CaADP kinetically limits ADP-to-ATP exchange and consequently ATP-enhanced dissociation of BiP from substrates.
source: This observation indicates that the slow release of CaADP kinetically limits ADP-to-ATP exchange and consequently ATP-enhanced dissociation of BiP from substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In solutions containing Mg2+ and a mixture of ATP and ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), the NEF Grp170 enhanced dissociation of BiP from substrate-loaded BLI sensors both in the absence and presence of Ca2+ to a similar extent (on average ~2.2- and~2.5-fold, respectively).
source: In solutions containing Mg2+ and a mixture of ATP and ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2), the NEF Grp170 enhanced dissociation of BiP from substrate-loaded BLI sensors both in the absence and presence of Ca2+ to a similar extent (on average ~2.2- and~2.5-fold, respectively; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ca2+ strongly inhibited MABA-ADP release from mammalian BiP and Drosophila BiP (by ∼79% and ∼82%, respectively) but had a more modest inhibitory effect on MABA-ADP release from DnaK (∼30%), cytosolic Hsp70 (∼37%), and Hsc70 (∼50%).
source: Ca2+ strongly inhibited MABA-ADP release from mammalian BiP and Drosophila BiP (by ∼79% and ∼82%, respectively) but had a more modest inhibitory effect on MABA-ADP release from DnaK (∼30%), cytosolic Hsp70 (∼37%), and Hsc70 (∼50%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ had the strongest inhibitory effect on the dissociation of mammalian BiP (∼43% decreased dissociation rate) and Drosophila BiP (∼53% decrease) from BLI sensors, whereas dissociation of the other chaperones was less affected (Hsp70 ∼16%, Hsc70 ∼16%, DnaK ∼9% decrease).
source: Dissociation was performed in the presence of Mg2+, ATP, and ADP ([ATP]/[ADP]=2). Further addition of Ca2+ had the strongest inhibitory effect on the dissociation of mammalian BiP (∼43% decreased dissociation rate) and Drosophila BiP (∼53% decrease), whereas dissociation of the other chaperones was less affected (Hsp70 ∼16%, Hsc70 ∼16%, DnaK ∼9% decrease; Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Sensitivity of nucleotide exchange and substrate interactions to Ca2+ is a feature that is relatively selective to BiP homologues.
source: These observations suggest that sensitivity of nucleotide exchange and substrate interactions to Ca2+ is a feature that is relatively selective to BiP homologues, perhaps having evolved as an adaptation to the ER environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 5A, B, and C.

claim: High-resolution X-ray crystal structures were obtained for the NBDs of mammalian BiP, Hsp70, and Hsc70 co-crystallised with Ca2+ and ADP.
source: To establish if the selective effect of Ca2+ on ADP binding to BiP is reflected in the structure of the complex, we purified the NBDs of mammalian BiP, Hsp70, and Hsc70 and co-crystallised them with Ca2+ and ADP. High-resolution X-ray crystal structures were obtained for all three NBDs (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: In each NBD structure, additional density in the nucleotide-binding cleft indicated occupancy by ADP.
source: In each case, additional density in the nucleotide-binding cleft indicated occupancy by ADP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and the overall conformations of the three NBDs were very similar (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6A.

claim: Overlay of the BiP(NBD) structure with the Hsp70(NBD) and Hsc70(NBD) structures revealed root-mean-squared deviations (RMSD) of 0.769 Å and 0.734 Å over the Cα alignment, respectively.
source: Overlay of the BiP(NBD) structure with the Hsp70(NBD) and Hsc70(NBD) structures revealed root-mean-squared deviations (RMSD) of 0.769 Å and 0.734 Å over the Cα alignment, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data analysis.

claim: In each NBD structure, Ca2+ was identified in the nucleotide-binding cleft, where it formed contacts to both phosphate groups (α and β) of the nucleotide as well as indirect contacts to protein residues via several water molecules.
source: Moreover, in each structure, Ca2+ was identified in the nucleotide- binding cleft, where it formed contacts to both phosphate groups (α and β) of the nucleotide as well as indirect contacts to protein residues via several water molecules (Figure 6A, inset).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The position of the Ca2+ ion and the coordinated water molecules were nearly identical in all three NBD complexes and similar to a previously reported lower resolution structure of human BiP bound to CaADP.
source: The position of the Ca2+ ion and the coordinated water molecules were nearly identical in all three complexes and similar to a previously reported lower resolution structure of human BiP bound to CaADP (Wisniewska et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Mg2+ ion in an earlier Hsc70(NBD)•Mg2+•ADP structure coordinates only the β-phosphate of ADP directly.
source: In contrast, the Mg2+ ion in an earlier Hsc70(NBD)•Mg2+•ADP structure coordinates only the β-phosphate of ADP directly (Figure 6B, upper panel), which may contribute to the lower affinity of MgADP compared to CaADP for NBD binding.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6B and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Ca2+ participates in the coordination of ADP in the NBD, which is consistent with cooperative binding of Ca2+ and nucleotide to BiP.
source: Together, these findings reveal that Ca2+ participates in the coordination of ADP in the NBD, which is consistent with cooperative binding of Ca2+ and nucleotide to BiP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The structures imply that binding of Ca2+ and Mg2+ is mutually exclusive.
source: The structures also imply that binding of Ca2+ and Mg2+ is mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The IC50 values for Ca2+-dependent inhibition of MABA-ADP release from the NBDs of Hsp70 (444.7 ± 80.5 µM) and Hsc70 (345.5 ± 71.1 µM) were much higher than from the NBD of BiP (57.1 ± 7.4 µM).
source: However, the IC50 values for Ca2+-dependent inhibition of MABA-ADP release from the NBDs of Hsp70 (444.7 ± 80.5 µM) and Hsc70 (345.5 ± 71.1 µM) were much higher than from the NBD of BiP (57.1 ± 7.4 µM) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The IC50 for inhibition of MABA-ADP release from DnaK(NBD) by Ca2+ was so high (>8 mM) that saturation was not reached over the titration range.
source: In contrast, the IC50 for inhibition of MABA-ADP release from DnaK(NBD) by Ca2+ was so high (>8 mM) that saturation was not reached over the titration range (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The IC50 for inhibition of MABA-ADP release from Kar2 NBD by Ca2+ was 888.0 ± 233.6 µM.
source: We also tested the NBD of Kar2, the ER Hsp70 chaperone of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), which had a high IC50 of 888.0 ± 233.6 µM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Regulation by Ca2+ seems specific to metazoan BiP.
source: Thus, regulation by Ca2+ seems specific to metazoan BiP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing different Hsp70s.

claim: Binding of ADP to all NBDs substantially elevated their melting temperatures (Tm).
source: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) measurements revealed that binding of ADP to all NBDs substantially elevated their melting temperatures (Tm), as observed previously for full-length BiP (Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Tm of NBDs increased further in the presence of Ca2+.
source: The Tm increased further in the presence of Ca2+ (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The stabilising effect of Ca2+ was greatest for mammalian and Drosophila BiP(NBD), compared to the cytosolic Hsp70(NBD)s.
source: Importantly, the stabilising effect of Ca2+ was greatest for mammalian and Drosophila BiP(NBD), compared to the cytosolic Hsp70(NBD)s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The larger decrease in structural flexibility imparted by CaADP binding to the NBD of ER-localised Hsp70s contributes to the relatively stronger inhibition of ADP release by Ca2+.
source: These findings suggest that the larger decrease in structural flexibility imparted by CaADP binding to the NBD of ER-localised Hsp70s contributes to the relatively stronger inhibition of ADP release by Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: BiP oligomers are based on typical substrate interactions between the SBD of one protomer and the interdomain linker of another protomer.
source: These homomeric BiP complexes are based on typical substrate interactions between the SBD of one protomer and the interdomain linker of another protomer (Preissler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All BiP molecules of an oligomer are in a post-hydrolysis, domain-undocked state typical of ADP-bound or apo Hsp70s.
source: As a consequence, all BiP molecules of an oligomer are in a post-hydrolysis, domain-undocked state typical of ADP-bound or apo Hsp70s (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure and properties of BiP oligomers.

claim: In BiP oligomers, only the first BiP molecule (A) can bind substrate, whereas the SBDs and linkers of all internal protomers (B) are occupied.
source: These features entail a chain-like configuration where only the first BiP molecule (A) can bind substrate, whereas the SBDs and linkers of all internal protomers (B) are occupied.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure and properties of BiP oligomers.

claim: Oligomer assembly and disassembly occur mainly on one end and involve the 'C' protomer because it provides a binding site for another BiP molecule (in assembly) and is the only protomer able to undergo ATP-induced domain docking (required for dissociation).
source: This model also predicts that oligomer assembly and disassembly occur mainly on one end and involve the 'C' protomer because it provides a binding site for another BiP molecule (in assembly) and is the only protomer able to undergo ATP-induced domain docking (required for dissociation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure and properties of BiP oligomers.

claim: Crystals of BiP were obtained in multi-component mixtures formed by substrate interactions between the SBD and the interdomain linker of adjacent molecules in the crystal lattice.
source: The strong propensity of BiP to form oligomers and their architecture is further supported by structural data: despite being C-terminally truncated beyond helix A of the flexible SBD lid structure and containing a substrate binding-weakening V461F mutation, we obtained crystals of BiP in multi-component mixtures formed by substrate interactions between the SBD and the interdomain linker of adjacent molecules in the crystal lattice (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: BiP oligomers rapidly disassemble in vitro in the presence of ATP.
source: BiP oligomers rapidly disassemble in vitro in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BiP oligomers.

claim: Specific inactivation of the 'C' protomer at the (+)-end would render BiP oligomers refractory to the destabilising effect of ATP.
source: However, the hypothesised process by which BiP oligomers form and disassemble, described above, predicts that specific inactivation of the 'C' protomer at the (+)-end would render them refractory to the destabilising effect of ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model of BiP oligomer structure and dynamics.

claim: Under conditions that favour oligomers, a large fraction of BiP is resistant to cleavage by SubA, likely because only the linker of the 'C' protomer is accessible to the protease, whereas the linkers of all other protomers are protected by an SBD of another BiP protomer.
source: Under conditions that favour oligomers, a large fraction of BiP is resistant to cleavage by SubA (Preissler et al., 2015), likely because only the linker of the 'C' protomer is accessible to the protease, whereas the linkers of all other protomers are protected by an SBD of another BiP protomer (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and inference based on the model of BiP oligomer structure.

claim: Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) analysis after exposure of BiP to SubA revealed a shift of all peaks to later elution times, consistent with removal of a single NBD from oligomeric structures and complete cleavage of monomers.
source: Indeed, size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) analysis after exposure of BiP to SubA revealed a shift of all peaks to later elution times, consistent with removal of a single NBD from oligomeric structures and complete cleavage of monomers (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The fluorescently-labelled substrate peptide co-eluted with BiP monomers and oligomers in SEC.
source: The peptide co-eluted with BiP monomers and oligomers (Figure 7D, left panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The stepwise increase in the ratio of A230 to fluorescence signal with oligomer size is consistent with each oligomeric species exposing only a single binding site [at its (-)-end].
source: The stepwise increase in the ratio of A230 to fluorescence signal with oligomer size is consistent with each oligomeric species exposing only a single binding site [at its (-)-end].
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Addition of ATP to the sample shortly before injection into the SEC column converted BiP oligomers largely into monomers, releasing the bound substrate peptide.
source: As expected, addition of ATP to the sample shortly before injection into the SEC column converted BiP oligomers largely into monomers, releasing the bound substrate peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Treatment with SubA prior to SEC shifted the oligomer peaks to later elution times and abolished the monomer signal in both the A230 and fluorescence channel.
source: As noted previously, treatment with SubA prior to SEC shifted the oligomer peaks to later elution times and abolished the monomer signal in both the A230 and fluorescence channel.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In contrast to the intact oligomers, the SubA-cleaved species were completely insensitive to ATP-induced disassembly and peptide release.
source: However, in contrast to the intact oligomers, the cleaved species were completely insensitive to ATP-induced disassembly and peptide release (Figure 7D, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Proteolytic removal of the NBD from the terminal protomer stabilises BiP oligomers by inactivating their only conformationally responsive molecule, the 'C' protomer at the (+)-end.
source: We conclude that proteolytic removal of the NBD from the terminal protomer stabilises BiP oligomers by inactivating their only conformationally responsive molecule, the 'C' protomer at the (+)-end.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: These data provide evidence for a strictly directional oligomer disassembly mode that proceeds from the (+)-end.
source: These data also provide evidence for a strictly directional oligomer disassembly mode that proceeds from the (+)-end.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MABA-ADP (bound in the presence of Mg2+) dissociated from stabilised (SubA-cleaved) BiP oligomers and untreated BiP at similar rates.
source: MABA-ADP (bound in the presence of Mg2+) dissociated from stabilised (SubA-cleaved) BiP oligomers and untreated BiP at similar rates (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) had a similar inhibitory effect on MABA-ADP dissociation from both stabilised BiP oligomers and untreated BiP.
source: Addition of Ca2+ ([MgCl2]/[CaCl2]=3) had a similar inhibitory effect on MABA-ADP dissociation from both samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Under conditions with Ca2+ present, Grp170 enhanced the rate of MABA-ADP release from stabilised oligomers only ∼2.9-fold, whereas release from untreated BiP was enhanced ∼12.3-fold.
source: In contrast, under these conditions, Grp170 enhanced the rate of MABA-ADP release from stabilised oligomers only ∼2.9-fold, whereas release from untreated BiP was enhanced ∼12.3-fold (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Passive nucleotide exchange occurs with normal rates on BiP oligomers but their conformationally trapped state renders them non-responsive to ATP binding.
source: These results indicate (i) that passive nucleotide exchange occurs with normal rates on BiP oligomers but their conformationally trapped state renders them non-responsive to ATP binding, and (ii) that oligomers are largely resistant to Grp170-stimulated nucleotide release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: BiP oligomers are largely resistant to Grp170-stimulated nucleotide release.
source: These results indicate (i) that passive nucleotide exchange occurs with normal rates on BiP oligomers but their conformationally trapped state renders them non-responsive to ATP binding, and (ii) that oligomers are largely resistant to Grp170-stimulated nucleotide release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The relative inertness of the internal protomers kinetically favours BiP oligomers over other BiP-substrate interactions in the Ca2+-depleted ER.
source: Together with the finding that BiP oligomers disassemble from one end, these observations suggest a mechanism whereby the relative inertness of the internal protomers kinetically favours BiP oligomers over other BiP-substrate interactions in the Ca2+-depleted ER.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the model of BiP oligomer dynamics.

claim: In the Ca2+-depleted ER, BiP-substrate interactions are destabilised.
source: In the Ca2+-depleted ER, BiP-substrate interactions are destabilised (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The partitioning of substrates away from BiP favours trafficking of those substrates that would otherwise have been retained by BiP, whilst promoting de-repression of the UPR transducers.
source: The partitioning of substrates away from the only luminal Hsp70 favours trafficking of those substrates that would otherwise have been retained by BiP, whilst promoting de-repression of the UPR transducers, themselves BiP substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the known role of BiP in UPR regulation.

claim: The perturbation to ER proteostasis is compounded by the polarity of BiP oligomers, which specifies their relative inertness to Ca2+ fluctuations, thus kinetically driving BiP to oligomerise and depleting the pool of active monomers.
source: The perturbation to ER proteostasis is compounded by the polarity of BiP oligomers, which specifies their relative inertness to Ca2+ fluctuations, thus kinetically driving BiP to oligomerise and depleting the pool of active monomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on BiP oligomers.

claim: Regulation of BiP by Ca2+ co-evolved with the functions of the mammalian ER in Ca2+ storage and signalling.
source: Comparison of cytosolic and ER Hsp70s suggests that regulation of BiP by Ca2+ co-evolved with the functions of the mammalian ER in Ca2+ storage and signalling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative experimental data on different Hsp70s.

claim: The yeast ER Hsp70 Kar2 is much less sensitive to Ca2+ than its metazoan counterparts, despite sharing ∼72% sequence identity in the NBD.
source: In this vein, the yeast ER Hsp70 Kar2 is of special interest, as we found it to be much less sensitive to Ca2+ than its metazoan counterparts, despite sharing ∼72% sequence identity in the NBD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The yeast vacuole, not the ER, serves as the major intracellular Ca2+ store responsible for regulating Ca2+ release.
source: This correlates with the yeast vacuole, not the ER, serving as the major intracellular Ca2+ store responsible for regulating Ca2+ release (Denis and Cyert, 2002; Halachmi and Eilam, 1989; Strayle et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At high CaADP concentrations, the crystallised NBDs of all Hsp70's tested bind the cation-nucleotide complex indistinguishably.
source: At high CaADP concentrations, the crystallised NBDs of all Hsp70's tested bind the cation-nucleotide complex indistinguishably.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Subtle differences in protein dynamics, arising from the 30% sequence divergence between the NBD of metazoan BiP and its cytosolic counterparts, may account for their different sensitivity to Ca2+.
source: Solution-based assays suggest that subtle differences in protein dynamics, arising from the 30% sequence divergence between the NBD of metazoan BiP and its cytosolic counterparts, may account for their different sensitivity to Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing different Hsp70s.

claim: The destabilising effect of ER Ca2+ depletion on BiP-substrate complexes may have arisen as a response to situations in which the demands for bulk protein export from the ER outweighs the benefits of stringent quality control.
source: The destabilising effect of ER Ca2+ depletion on BiP-substrate complexes may have arisen as a response to situations in which the demands for bulk protein export from the ER (to replenish secreted protein stores) outweighs the benefits of stringent quality control (that would otherwise be imposed by more prolonged BiP-substrate interactions and ER retention).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The dissociation of BiP from a class of not yet natively assembled but export-ready substrates during Ca2+ signalling events may reflect a mechanism for tuning the stringency of quality control to physiological demands.
source: The dissociation of BiP from a class of not yet natively assembled but export-ready substrates during Ca2+ signalling events may thus reflect a mechanism for tuning the stringency of quality control to physiological demands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Declining ER Ca2+ favours dissociation of BiP from UPR signal transducers, which is consistent with previous pulldown experiments showing release of BiP from PERK and ATF6 upon ER Ca2+ depletion.
source: The findings presented here imply that declining ER Ca2+ favours dissociation of BiP from UPR signal transducers, which is consistent with previous pulldown experiments showing release of BiP from PERK and ATF6 upon ER Ca2+ depletion (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Shen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: BiP dissociation under conditions of ER Ca2+ depletion is complete on a timescale of minutes and does not require an ongoing supply of nascent unfolded proteins.
source: Importantly, BiP dissociation under these conditions is complete on a timescale of minutes and does not require an ongoing supply of nascent unfolded proteins, placing it upstream of any proteostatic challenge arising directly from Ca2+ depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior observations.

claim: The Ca2+-entrained pulses of UPR signalling arising from the specialised sensitivity of BiP to Ca2+ may have evolved to tune gene expression programs that build secretory capacity to the secretory activity of cells.
source: The Ca2+-entrained pulses of UPR signalling arising from the specialised sensitivity of BiP to Ca2+ may have evolved to tune gene expression programs that build secretory capacity to the secretory activity of cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ acts mainly on the nucleotide exchange phase of BiP's chaperone cycle.
source: Our findings indicate that Ca2+ acts mainly on the nucleotide exchange phase of BiP's chaperone cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: After post-hydrolysis ADP release, ATP and ADP compete for binding to BiP.
source: After post-hydrolysis ADP release, ATP and ADP compete for binding to BiP (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BiP's chaperone cycle, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Ca2+ enhances the affinity of ADP for BiP and thereby promotes the ADP-bound state during nucleotide exchange.
source: Ca2+ enhances the affinity of ADP for BiP and thereby promotes the ADP-bound state during nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The efficiency of ADP-to-ATP exchange and rates of substrate release are inversely related to [Ca2+].
source: The efficiency of ADP-to-ATP exchange and rates of substrate release are thus inversely related to [Ca2+].
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: As BiP requires MgATP to re-enter its chaperone cycle, the rate at which ATP hydrolysis-dependent interactions with substrates are formed remain largely unaffected by Ca2+.
source: As BiP requires MgATP to re-enter its chaperone cycle (Kassenbrock and Kelly, 1989), the rate at which ATP hydrolysis-dependent interactions with substrates are formed remain largely unaffected by Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: A decrease in [Ca2+] enhances the effective rate of ATP-induced substrate release from BiP relative to the rate of substrate binding, leading to a net decline of BiP•substrate complexes.
source: This rationalises the observed consequences of lowering free Ca2+ levels in the ER on the interactions of BiP with its substrates: a decrease in [Ca2+] enhances the effective rate of ATP-induced substrate release from BiP relative to the rate of substrate binding, leading to a net decline of BiP•substrate complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ binds in the nucleotide-binding cleft of the NBD and participates in coordinating the phosphate groups of ADP.
source: Our structural data show that Ca2+ binds in the nucleotide-binding cleft of the NBD and participates in coordinating the phosphate groups of ADP.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 6.

claim: This sufficiently explains the observed cooperative binding mode of Ca2+ and nucleotide to BiP.
source: This sufficiently explains the observed cooperative binding mode of Ca2+ and nucleotide to BiP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Mutation of the second metal-binding site did not affect the responsiveness of BiP to Ca2+ in ADP release experiments, rendering its relevance to any allosteric regulation of BiP by Ca2+ improbable.
source: Moreover, mutation of the second metal-binding site did not affect the responsiveness of BiP to Ca2+ in ADP release experiments, rendering its relevance to any allosteric regulation of BiP by Ca2+ improbable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Chaperones, in particular BiP, are the most abundant ATPases in the ER.
source: Chaperones, in particular BiP, are the most abundant ATPases in the ER (Bakunts et al., 2017; Dierks et al., 1996; Itzhak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increasing protein folding load could boost ATP consumption by chaperones and temporarily lower the luminal ATP:ADP ratio.
source: Increasing protein folding load could thus boost ATP consumption by chaperones and temporarily lower the luminal ATP:ADP ratio.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about chaperone function.

claim: Coupling regulation of BiP by Ca2+ to the ATP:ADP ratio may save energy at basally high luminal [Ca2+] by amplifying the effect of ADP as a competitor for ATP and thus lowering BiP's ATPase activity.
source: Coupling regulation of BiP by Ca2+ to the ATP:ADP ratio may therefore save energy at basally high luminal [Ca2+] by amplifying the effect of ADP as a competitor for ATP and thus lowering BiP's ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: ER Ca2+ depletion might enhance BiP's ATPase activity.
source: In contrast, ER Ca2+ depletion might enhance BiP's ATPase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: BiP oligomerisation may have evolved to alleviate the consequences of enhanced ATP consumption at low Ca2+ levels by sequestering BiP in inactive complexes with relatively slow turnover rates under these conditions.
source: Likewise, BiP oligomerisation may have evolved to alleviate the consequences of enhanced ATP consumption at low Ca2+ levels by sequestering BiP in inactive complexes with relatively slow turnover rates under these conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: BiP oligomer disassembly proceeds in a strictly directional manner and thus might be relatively slow compared to the one-step dissociation of heterodimeric BiP•substrate complexes.
source: Mechanistically, this can be explained by the finding that BiP oligomer disassembly proceeds in a strictly directional manner and thus might be relatively slow compared to the one-step dissociation of heterodimeric BiP•substrate complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on BiP oligomers.

claim: At low [Ca2+] when ADP-to-ATP exchange is more efficient, the unidirectional, step-wise dissociation of BiP oligomers imposes an even greater relative kinetic penalty, causing a redistribution of BiP from heterodimeric BiP•substrate complexes to oligomers.
source: This difference is likely enhanced at low [Ca2+] when ADP-to-ATP exchange is more efficient and the unidirectional, step-wise dissociation of BiP oligomers imposes an even greater relative kinetic penalty, causing a redistribution of BiP from heterodimeric BiP•substrate complexes to oligomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on BiP oligomers.

claim: Conformationally trapped oligomeric BiP is largely resistant to stimulated ADP release by Grp170.
source: Furthermore, conformationally trapped oligomeric BiP is largely resistant to stimulated ADP release by Grp170, the most abundant NEF in the ER (Behnke et al., 2015; Weitzmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and citations to prior literature.

claim: Part of the Grp170-binding site on BiP is likely sterically occluded in oligomers.
source: Grp170 belongs to the Hsp110 class of NEFs, which bind Hsp70s via a large contact area (Polier et al., 2008). It is therefore likely that part of the Grp170-binding site on BiP is sterically occluded in oligomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about Grp170 and the structure of BiP oligomers, supported by a citation.

claim: The differential action of Grp170 (and potentially other co-factors) on BiP•substrate complexes and oligomers likely contributes to the altered BiP dynamics at varying Ca2+ levels.
source: The differential action of Grp170 (and potentially other co-factors) on BiP•substrate complexes and oligomers likely contributes to the altered BiP dynamics at varying Ca2+ levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.
